\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty}
\label{ch:hi-numbers-eleven-to-twenty}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from eleven to twenty in Hindi and spot the subtractive nineteen sitting inside the list.}

Count \hi{ग्यारह} to \hi{बीस}, then read \hi{उन्नीस} as 'one less than twenty', the same logic as Latin's ūndēvīgintī.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{ग्यारह} — \hi{बीस}]{\hi{ग्यारह}, \hi{बीस} — genuinely irregular, and one honest exception}

\label{lesson:HI-C22-gyarah-bees}



\begin{quote}
Be honest about this one: Hindi's teens don't follow a clean, predictable pattern the way Spanish's or Latin's do. But hiding inside that irregularity is a real echo of something Latin does too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — Eleven to twenty}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
11 & \textbf{\hi{ग्यारह}} & \emph{gyārah} \\
12 & \textbf{\hi{बारह}} & \emph{bārah} \\
13 & \textbf{\hi{तेरह}} & \emph{terah} \\
14 & \textbf{\hi{चौदह}} & \emph{chaudah} \\
15 & \textbf{\hi{पंद्रह}} & \emph{pandrah} \\
16 & \textbf{\hi{सोलह}} & \emph{solah} \\
17 & \textbf{\hi{सत्रह}} & \emph{satrah} \\
18 & \textbf{\hi{अठारह}} & \emph{aṭhārah} \\
19 & \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} & \emph{unnīs} \\
20 & \textbf{\hi{बीस}} & \emph{bīs} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The two words — Honest irregularity}
Unlike Spanish's transparent \emph{dieciséis}-\emph{diecinueve} or even the fused-but- regular \emph{once}-\emph{quince}, Hindi's 11-18 each descend from their own Sanskrit number-word (\emph{ekādaśa, dvādaśa, trayodaśa}...) through centuries of individually unpredictable erosion. Most end in \textbf{-rah}, a worn-down echo of Sanskrit's \textquotedblleft{}-daśa\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}), but the erosion of each number's front half isn't predictable from the number itself — these genuinely have to be memorized one by one, the way English speakers just memorize \textquotedblleft{}eleven\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}twelve\textquotedblright{} rather than deriving them.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{उन्नीस}}
Here's the honest exception: \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} (\emph{unnīs}, 19) most likely isn't simply a worn-down \textquotedblleft{}nine-ten\textquotedblright{} — it likely continues Sanskrit's \textbf{own} special, \textbf{subtractive} name for 19: \textbf{\hi{ऊनविंशति}} (\emph{ūnaviṃśati}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one less than twenty}\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{ūna}, \textquotedblleft{}less, deficient,\textquotedblright{} + \emph{viṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} — a later, shortened form of the fuller Vedic \emph{ekonaviṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}one-less-twenty,\textquotedblright{} with the \emph{eka}, \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} eventually dropped). Sanskrit used this same \emph{ūna-}/ \emph{ekona-} (\textquotedblleft{}one-less-than\textquotedblright{}) subtractive pattern for every number ending in 9 up through 99 — 29, 49, 99, all named as \textquotedblleft{}one less than\textquotedblright{} the next round number.

This is a genuine, striking parallel to something you already met: \textbf{Latin's own ūndēvīgintī} (\textquotedblleft{}one from twenty\textquotedblright{}) for 19, from the numbers-11-20 lesson. Two completely unrelated language families — Indo-Aryan and Italic, both descended from Proto-Indo-European but separated for thousands of years — independently landed on the exact same subtractive logic for naming nineteen.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{बीस}}
\textbf{\hi{बीस}} (\emph{bīs}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}) continues Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{विंशति}} (\emph{viṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gyārah, bārah, terah\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12, 13, each individually memorized
  \item \textquotedblleft{}unnīs\textquotedblright{} — 19, most likely \textquotedblleft{}one less than twenty\textquotedblright{} (ūnaviṃśati), echoing Latin's ūndēvīgintī
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bīs\textquotedblright{} — twenty
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do Hindi's numbers 11-18 follow a predictable pattern the way Spanish's teens do? (\textbf{No} — each is individually eroded from its own Sanskrit ancestor and must be memorized.) What does \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} most likely preserve from Sanskrit, and what does it mean? (Sanskrit's \textbf{subtractive} \emph{ūnaviṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one less than twenty}.\textquotedblright{}) What Latin number from an earlier lesson uses the exact same subtractive logic? (\textbf{ūndēvīgintī}, \textquotedblleft{}one from twenty\textquotedblright{} — two unrelated language families, the same idea.)
\end{tcolorbox}
